This method computes the initial microflake parameters—density $\rho_0$ and self-shadowing $A_0$—for a low-resolution voxel such that its directional transparencies match those of the input high-resolution voxel block along the principal axes [S1].

The claim states that the method computes initial microflake parameters (density ρ0 and self-shadowing A0) for a low-resolution voxel to match directional transparencies of the input high-resolution voxel block along principal axes. Source [S1] explicitly confirms this in Section 7.4.1, stating that the goal is to compute ρ0 and A0 such that 'directional transparencies of the low-res voxel matches exactly T(ωx), T(ωy) and T(ωz), the transparencies of the block of input voxels.' The notes and passages detail the specific algorithms (Iso and Aniso) used to derive these parameters based on the principal axes (X, Y, Z).
supported
Both algorithms only consider the principal axes, potentially missing directional information in other orientations [S1].

The evidence explicitly states that both Algorithm Iso and Algorithm Aniso compute their parameters (density ρ0 and self-shadowing A0) based on the directional transparencies along the three principal axes (X, Y, Z). Algorithm Iso averages the density across these three axes, while Algorithm Aniso uses the maximum density among these three axes and computes anisotropic parameters specifically for these axes. Neither algorithm considers directional information from other orientations outside of these principal axes. Therefore, the claim that they 'only consider the principal axes' is fully supported by the text.
